assessment.nobel_worthiness: The credit-cycles framework shows how collateral constraints turn small shocks into persistent, amplified fluctuations. It became a core building block of macro-finance and of the modern analysis of financial crises and balance-sheet channels. The ideas are foundational and widely taught, and they gave a mechanism to later quantitative work.
assessment.attribution: The core idea is the 1997 Kiyotaki–Moore credit-cycles paper. The financial-accelerator strand (Bernanke, Gertler, Gilchrist) is related but separate, and Bernanke is already a laureate for banks and financial crises. I therefore credit the two originators of the collateral-constraint amplification mechanism and leave Gertler and Gilchrist off the proposed set.
assessment.maturity: The work is nearly three decades old, was validated by the 2007–09 crisis, and has been extended many times. It is mature, and the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises does not cover the collateral-constrained amplification mechanism itself.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises may weigh against it.
Whether the committee would prefer to include Gertler as part of a broader financial-frictions award.
Empirical quantification of the mechanism is still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work built modern political economics by putting electoral rules, constitutions, and state capacity into formal and empirical models of fiscal and growth outcomes. It changed how economists treat institutions and policy choice as endogenous. It is highly influential across public economics, development, and macro.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central figures, through their joint research programme and book. Besley's contributions on accountability, state capacity, and development politics are substantial and complementary. The three-person set is coherent, but the credit split is not perfectly symmetric.
assessment.maturity: The programme spans three decades, with extensive empirical confirmation and a large follow-on literature. It is mature, and the 2024 institutions prize does not duplicate its formal political-economy contribution.
uncertainties: The 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity may be seen as overlapping thematically.
Empirical identification of constitutional effects is contested.
Whether the committee would limit the award to two names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection changed international trade by showing that gains from trade operate through reallocation across firms, not only across industries. The framework reshaped empirical trade, links to productivity and inequality, and underlies much of current trade policy analysis. Its measurable implications have been tested extensively.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the key paper, and Helpman contributed the broader heterogeneous-firm and trade-and-inequality agenda. Redding, Bernard, Eaton, Kortum, and others are also important, so the credit is diffuse. The two-person proposal reflects the primary originator and a leading architect of the field.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of confirmation in firm-level data across countries. Timing is mature, and Krugman's 2008 prize covered the earlier new trade theory rather than this generation.
uncertainties: Credit is diffuse across Eaton–Kortum, Bernard–Jensen, and Melitz.
Helpman may be considered mainly under the separate trade-policy or growth contributions.
Quantitative welfare gains from selection are model-dependent.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities, the New Keynesian synthesis, and the theory of rule-based monetary policy are the intellectual core of modern central banking and applied macro. The contribution is deep in theory, with major policy influence. As a macroeconomist I see the importance clearly, but field affinity is not evidence of merit, so I weigh it against the diffuse attribution.
assessment.attribution: The credit is highly diffuse. Calvo supplied the pricing device, Taylor the policy-rule insight and wage-contracting work, and Woodford the micro-founded policy framework. Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, and Smets also had important roles. Any three-person set will leave out major contributors.
assessment.maturity: The ideas are fully mature and have been tested through decades of policy practice, though the post-2008 and 2021–23 inflation episodes revised some of the framework.
uncertainties: Severe attribution difficulty and a risk of exclusion controversy.
The pandemic-era inflation challenged parts of the framework.
My own research proximity to menu costs and macro may bias my view, which I disclose and do not adjudicate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the empirical study of trade shocks transformed the understanding of wage inequality, polarisation, and local labour-market adjustment. The work is both conceptually and empirically influential, and it has strong policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Katz's work on skill-biased change with Goldin and others, Autor's task framework, and Autor–Dorn–Hanson on the China shock form a plausible cluster. The task-model theory also has important non-listed contributors, and Dorn is excluded from the proposed set. The credit is plausible but not clean.
assessment.maturity: The research spans roughly 25 years. The China-shock results have been replicated and debated, while the automation and AI implications are still unfolding.
uncertainties: The theoretical task framework has contributions beyond the credited set.
Goldin's 2023 prize and Acemoglu's 2024 prize covered adjacent ground.
The long-run persistence of trade-shock effects is debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation research programme gave a disciplined, measurable account of how distortions to resource allocation across firms explain cross-country productivity gaps. It linked micro data to aggregate growth and development outcomes and reoriented development macro. Its quantitative method is widely adopted.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh–Klenow (2009) is the benchmark paper. Restuccia–Rogerson (2008) are close co-originators, but Rogerson is not credited in this entry. Banerjee–Duflo and others on misallocation also contributed, so the credit is somewhat contested.
assessment.maturity: The agenda is about 15–20 years old, with substantial follow-up, and the core measurements are still debated, which suggests the field is not fully settled.
uncertainties: Measurement error and the interpretation of dispersion in marginal products are contested.
Omission of Rogerson, a co-originator, within the credited set.
Growth-theory work has been recognised recently, so there may be topic fatigue.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data gave the first credible, granular maps of intergenerational mobility and its spatial and causal drivers. This changed empirical public economics and has had major policy impact. Methodological and substantive contributions are both substantial.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is clearly the central figure. Hendren and Friedman are major co-authors, but the credit for individual papers is spread across a large team. The proposed set is plausible but depends on how the committee reads the division of labour.
assessment.maturity: The work is roughly a decade old. It is influential but still young in terms of long-run replication and policy validation. I disclose that I work on social mobility myself and do not adjudicate that.
uncertainties: Relatively recent, with limited time for confirmation of causal-neighbourhood claims.
Debate over the causal interpretation of place effects.
Possible conflict from my own mobility research, which I disclose and do not adjudicate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural demand estimation with differentiated products, together with dynamic industry models, made merger analysis, competition policy, and market-power measurement empirically operational. The methods became the standard toolkit in industrial organisation and are used by antitrust agencies.
assessment.attribution: Berry–Levinsohn–Pakes (1995) is the benchmark demand paper, and Pakes's dynamic-model contributions add depth. Bresnahan, Ericson–Pakes, Olley–Pakes, Reiss, and others are also important, so the credit is broad. The three-person set is natural but excludes important contributors.
assessment.maturity: The methods have thirty years of widespread use and are mature. Core assumptions are well studied.
uncertainties: Many strong contributors are outside the three-name set.
Whether the committee views the contribution as primarily methodological.
Sensitivity of results to functional-form and instrument choices.
